meta.title: Global Crude Flow Intelligence Dashboard
meta.week_convention: Weeks run Monday-Sunday; week_ending is always the Sunday, with data captured up to the 09:00 Europe/Nicosia (Cyprus time) cutoff that Sunday morning.
meta.note: Built from free/public sources (EIA, IEA, OPEC, operator statements, Reuters/Al Jazeera/Bloomberg/OilPrice/Argus/Kpler-cited reporting) plus a seed route database. No live Kpler/Vortexa feed is connected in this build; flow figures are research snapshots, not real-time AIS-derived data. See each item's confidence tag and source.

Brief mid-September disruption: Petroleum Facilities Guard members shut the Hamada-Zawiya pipeline valve and halted Hamada/Tahara field output (~9-15 Sep) in a dispute over transferring the Guard from the defense ministry to NOC control, with NOC threatening force majeure; operations at the affected fields resumed within days and NOC does not expect further disruption, so the multi-year-high figure above is not revised.

weekly_flows.status: Shut down — drone attack, repairs underway
weekly_flows.event_explanation: Pipeline shut down 10-11 Sep 2026 after drone strikes hit Pump Stations 8 and 9 (~68 miles SE of Medina, ~30-acre burn scar, one complex burning 13+ hours); drones launched from Maysan province, Iraq (Iranian-aligned militants). This was Saudi Arabia's primary Hormuz-bypass route (~5 mb/d recent flow, ~7 mb/d nameplate), so the shutdown compounds the ongoing Hormuz crisis rather than relieving it. Aramco then suspended Yanbu crude loadings outright on 15 Sep and cancelled/delayed at least 3 European refiners' late-September cargoes (some pushed to November); every Aramco cargo for the last 10 days of September was reported at risk. Repair timeline estimates diverge sharply: Aramco/Bloomberg sources cite restoring ~half capacity within days via a bypass around the damaged section, with full capacity in ~5-6 weeks (matching separate Reuters sourcing and AP-sourced regional officials' "3-5 weeks"); US Energy Secretary Chris Wright called it "days"; satellite-imagery analysts argue the damage could take months. Saudi Arabia is compensating by increasing loadings through the Strait of Hormuz (incl. ship-to-ship transfers near Sohar, Oman) rather than restoring pipeline flow — Aramco reportedly sold ~20 million barrels to Asian refiners this week for lifting outside Hormuz. Treat mbd as 0 (pipeline flow) rather than terminal throughput, which may lag via stored buffer/rerouting.
weekly_flows.source: Wikipedia: 2026 East-West Crude Oil Pipeline attack; AP via PBS NewsHour; Engineering News-Record; Bloomberg; OilPrice.com; Al Jazeera (17 Sep 2026)

disruptions.description: "2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis": US/Israel strikes on Iran (Operation Epic Fury, 28 Feb 2026) triggered Iranian closure of the strait, ship boardings and mining. Ceasefire (8 Apr) failed; US naval blockade of Iranian ports (13 Apr-29 May); further escalation 5-6 Sept 2026 (US struck 3 Iranian tankers, Iran fired missiles at US warships). Brent spiked to $126 in March, to $96.28 on 6 Sept, then to $104.61 on 11 Sept (+8.7% week) as the Petroline shutdown (see disruption #6) compounded the crisis, and briefly to ~$108 on 15 Sept when Aramco suspended Yanbu loadings outright; prices eased somewhat by 17 Sept as Saudi Arabia shifted more volume through Hormuz. Saudi Arabia (-20% initially, now much deeper per disruption #6), Iraq (-70% at peak), Kuwait, Qatar, UAE and Iran all hit. Bypass routes (Saudi East-West/Yanbu, UAE Habshan-Fujairah, Iraq Kirkuk-Ceyhan) together carry only ~9 mb/d vs the ~20 mb/d the strait normally carries — and the Saudi bypass itself is now down (disruption #6). A planned Iran-Oman-GCC meeting to discuss a temporary Hormuz transit solution was postponed indefinitely as of 14 Sept with no new date set. The Persian Gulf Strait Authority (Iran) published an updated 14 Sept list of vessels it deems in violation of its transit protocols, threatening fines, detention or confiscation, and US forces have narrowed air-defence escort cover for tankers to two time slots a day.
disruptions.source: Wikipedia: 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis; Al Jazeera (6-7 Sep, 14 Sep, 17 Sep 2026); CNBC (16-17 Sep 2026); OilPrice.com (15 Sep 2026)

disruptions.description: Drone strikes on 10-11 Sep 2026 hit Pump Stations 8 and 9 of the East-West Pipeline (Petroline), causing fires (one complex burned 13+ hours, leaving a ~30-acre burn scar) and forcing a full shutdown on 11 Sep. Drones were traced to Maysan province, Iraq, launched by Iranian-aligned militants; Aramco has not detailed the exact equipment damaged. Petroline is Saudi Arabia's primary bypass route around the Strait of Hormuz (see disruption #1), carrying oil from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu — so this shutdown compounds the existing Hormuz crisis rather than offering relief from it, removing one of the few working bypass corridors. Aramco subsequently suspended Yanbu loadings outright (15 Sep) and cancelled/delayed European term cargoes, with every Aramco cargo for the last 10 days of September reported at risk (hitting PKN Orlen especially hard, ~40% of whose crude is Aramco-sourced). Rather than restoring pipeline flow, Saudi Arabia is compensating by routing more crude through the Strait of Hormuz itself, including ship-to-ship transfers near Sohar, Oman, reportedly with US military assistance — though this faces its own constraints (tanker rates near $1 million/day). This is distinct from the Hormuz crisis itself: it is a direct attack on Saudi domestic export infrastructure, not a transit blockade.
disruptions.source: Wikipedia: 2026 East-West Crude Oil Pipeline attack; AP via PBS NewsHour; Engineering News-Record; Bloomberg (14-16 Sep 2026); OilPrice.com (15-16 Sep 2026); Al Jazeera (17 Sep 2026); CNBC (15-17 Sep 2026)

disruptions.asset: Hamada-Zawiya crude pipeline / Hamada & Tahara fields
disruptions.location: Western Libya (Hamada-Zawiya pipeline and associated fields)
disruptions.event_type: Security force labour dispute / pipeline valve shutdown
disruptions.estimated_capacity_affected: Not disclosed at field level; Libya's total production is ~1.4 mb/d
disruptions.actual_flow_affected: Hamada and Tahara fields fully halted and Hamada-Zawiya pipeline valve closed for several days; partial cuts threatened at Wafa, Al-Khamsa and El Feel if demands unmet
disruptions.description: Members of Libya's Petroleum Facilities Guard shut a valve on the Hamada-Zawiya crude pipeline and halted output at the Hamada and Tahara fields (~9-10 Sep 2026), demanding the Guard be transferred financially and administratively from the defense ministry to the National Oil Corporation. NOC threatened to declare force majeure and warned of a full shutdown across additional fields (Wafa, Al-Khamsa, El Feel) if the valve was not reopened. Operations at the affected fields resumed within days and NOC does not anticipate further disruption; this reflects a recurring pattern of armed factions using oil infrastructure as leverage since 2011. Reported alongside the Saudi Petroline outage as a factor in a >$3 oil price jump around 15 Sep 2026.
